chapters.title: The Thermal Thesis: Kaori at the Intersection of AI Infrastructure and Taiwanese Precision Manufacturing
chapters.body:
Step inside a hyperscale data-center rack row outfitted with NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 systems and the first thing that strikes you is not the scale but the heat. Each seventy-two-GPU rack dissipates more than 120 kilowatts of thermal energy — roughly the output of a small residential street — and the laws of physics make air cooling an inadequate response. Fans cannot move sufficient mass fast enough; the only answer is liquid: precision-brazed copper and stainless manifolds running chilled coolant within centimetres of each silicon die, pulling heat away fast enough to keep accelerators at the operating temperatures that billion-dollar training runs demand.

The company that makes a critical piece of that thermal infrastructure is not a U.S. industrial conglomerate or a European engineering group. It is Kaori Heat Treatment Co., Ltd. (8996.TW), a fifty-five-year-old precision manufacturer headquartered in Zhongli District, Taoyuan City, Taiwan, whose vacuum-brazing furnaces have been producing heat exchangers since the year Richard Nixon flew to Beijing.

That longevity is the thesis. Kaori's five decades of metallurgical know-how — tempering stainless-steel plates, brazing copper alloys in controlled-atmosphere furnaces at temperatures exceeding 1,000°C, and sustaining the defect rates demanded by pressure-sensitive industrial applications — constitute a manufacturing moat that most entrants into the coolant distribution unit market cannot quickly replicate. The barrier is not conceptual complexity; it is the accumulated quality systems, furnace expertise, and process memory embedded in Kaori's Zhongli campus that make leak-free manifolds at operating pressures up to 10 bar economically producible at hyperscale volumes.

## Three Arcs, One Thread

Kaori's corporate history traces three overlapping strategic arcs, each building on the competencies assembled in the last. Founded in 1970 as an industrial heat-treatment and surface-processing foundry, the company spent its first quarter-century as a contract service provider to Taiwan's manufacturing base. In 1994 it pivoted into brazed plate heat exchangers (BPHEs), transforming itself from a service firm into a proprietary product manufacturer — a transition sealed by ISO certification, an export push into Europe, and a 1997 public listing. The third arc opened in 2009, when Kaori signed a technology-transfer agreement with Bloom Energy to manufacture solid-oxide fuel cell (SOFC) hotbox assemblies, importing precision high-temperature fabrication disciplines that would later prove directly transferable to AI data-center cooling products. Each arc preserved and deepened the core: vacuum brazing, precision metalworking, and thermal-fluid engineering.

## Snapshot Financials

The financial signature of the AI transition is legible in the revenue line.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (NTD) | Revenue (USD approx.) | Gross Margin |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 | 2.84B | ~89M | Low-to-mid 20s% |
| 2023 | 4.33B | ~136M | ~27% |
| 2024 | 4.00B | ~126M | ~26% |
| FY2025 | **6.58B** | **~207M** | **Peak ~33%** |

The 2024 contraction — revenue slipping from NTD 4.33 billion to NTD 4.00 billion — reflected the industry's pause between A100-generation builds and the GB200 production ramp. The 2025 explosion, a 64% surge to NTD 6.58 billion (~USD 207 million), reflected qualification wins converting to volume orders. By Q1 2026, monthly revenues had reached NTD 642 million in January, NTD 934 million in February, and NTD 1.27 billion in March — an aggregate run-rate of approximately 237% year-over-year growth. Management issued 2026 guidance of approximately 80% revenue growth, implying full-year revenues near NTD 11.8 billion. Market capitalisation peaked near NTD 112 billion (~USD 3.5 billion) on approximately 91.98 million shares, pricing the equity at roughly 79x trailing earnings.

## Two Independent Tailwinds

The investment thesis rests on two structural demand drivers that are independent and additive. The first is the AI industry's structural shift toward liquid cooling: industry data cited in Taiwanese financial media tracked liquid cooling's share of new data-centre deployments rising from approximately 18% in 2025 toward a projected 57–76% penetration in 2026, driven by thermal densities that air cooling cannot economically address in Blackwell and forthcoming Vera Rubin rack architectures. Kaori's CDU and coolant distribution manifold products — validated for NVIDIA GB200 NVL72, GB300, and ORV3 architectures, and identified by Morgan Stanley research as a key CDU supplier for Supermicro's GB200 platform — position the company directly in the path of that adoption curve.

The second tailwind is orthogonal: Bloom Energy's accelerating deployments of SOFC systems at AI data centres, supplying on-site power generation to facilities whose grid connections are increasingly constrained, created demand pull for Kaori hotbox assemblies that grew more than 50% year-over-year in fiscal 2025. Financial Vice President Wu Jun-Ying noted on the Q4 2025 earnings call that "order visibility is quite high, with current production and shipments being intensive." Cooling and power — two separate AI infrastructure problems, two separate revenue lines for one Zhongli manufacturer.

Whether Kaori's manufacturing moat proves deep enough to sustain a NTD 112 billion market capitalisation as Vertiv, Modine, and larger Asian fabricators accelerate their own entry into the CDU supply chain is the central analytical question this dossier sets out to answer.

chapters.title: Fifty-Five Years of Thermal Transformation: From H.S. Hans's German-Educated Furnace to NVIDIA's GB200 Supply Chain
chapters.body:
## The German Furnace and the Taoyuan Workshop

In the spring of 1970, a Taiwanese materials engineer named H.S. Hans returned from graduate studies in Germany and incorporated a small company in Hsin-Chuan city with registered capital of NTD 2.6 million. The enterprise, Kaori Heat Treatment Co., Ltd., occupied a niche that was unglamorous but structurally indispensable: industrial metal heat treatment and surface processing for Taiwan's rapidly expanding manufacturing base. Hans had studied the metallurgical sciences in West Germany at a moment when that country's Wirtschaftswunder was being built on precisely the kind of precision metalwork — controlled thermal cycling, case hardening, vacuum annealing — that Taiwanese industry was only beginning to demand. He imported not just knowledge but a engineering discipline: the conviction that controlling what happens to metal at elevated temperatures, at the molecular level, was a foundational competency rather than a commodity service.

The timing was propitious. Taiwan in 1970 was midway through its first industrial transformation, pivoting from labor-intensive textile and plastics manufacturing toward electronics assembly and precision metalwork. The government's export-processing zones were drawing foreign capital; domestic manufacturers needed reliable metal processing partners capable of meeting the tighter tolerances that export customers required. Kaori positioned itself at this intersection, and the business grew steadily. A second facility was opened in Kaohsiung in 1977 to serve the heavy industries clustered in southern Taiwan's port industrial zones. By 1987–1988, the company had substantially completed its primary manufacturing campus in the Zhongli District of Taoyuan — a deliberate choice of location that placed the company within the dense electronics and semiconductor supply chain corridors developing around Hsinchu. Japanese Industrial Standards marking approval followed in 1989, an early signal that management was thinking about export markets and quality certification rather than purely domestic service contracts.

## The BPHE Pivot: 1994 and the Logic of Product Ownership

The single most consequential strategic decision in Kaori's first fifty years came in 1994, when management resolved to establish a brazed plate heat exchanger division. The technology logic was clean: Kaori's existing vacuum brazing capability — the controlled, flux-free joining of metal components in a high-temperature furnace — was precisely the manufacturing process at the heart of a brazed plate heat exchanger's production. A BPHE is, at its core, a stack of precision-formed metal plates vacuum-brazed into a compact counter-flow heat exchanger; the company was already operating the furnaces and had developed the metallurgical intuition the process demanded. What the pivot added was proprietary product ownership. Rather than processing metal for other manufacturers, Kaori would design, certify, and sell a finished product under its own brand into growing HVAC and refrigeration markets across Asia and eventually Europe.

ISO 9002 certification for plate heat exchangers arrived in 1995, followed by CE and UL approvals that would open European and North American OEM channels. By 1997 the company had listed on the over-the-counter market with NTD 200 million in capital, using public markets to fund the tooling and certification investments that BPHE production required. The diversification was rational on multiple dimensions: it reduced dependence on service revenue cycles, created a product line with exportable intellectual property, and compelled the engineering team to internalize the thermal-fluid design disciplines — heat transfer coefficients, pressure drop optimization, working fluid compatibility — that would prove essential two decades later when data-center customers arrived with cooling specifications for GPU clusters.

## Bloom Energy and the American Quality Crucible

The partnership with Bloom Energy, which took shape through a technology-transfer agreement in approximately 2009, was formative in ways that extend well beyond its direct revenue contribution. Bloom Energy, founded in San Jose, California in 2001, was commercializing solid-oxide fuel cell technology that generated electricity through a ceramic electrochemical process operating at temperatures exceeding 700°C. The SOFC hotbox — the insulated assembly enclosing the fuel cell stack and its ancillary heat exchangers — required precision high-temperature brazing at specifications set not by Taiwan's industrial standards bodies but by an American engineering team building hardware for U.S. utility and commercial customers.

For Kaori, supplying hotbox assemblies to Bloom meant internalizing a quality system calibrated to the failure-tolerance levels of electrochemical power generation equipment: leaks were not commercial inconveniences but system failures. The discipline of manufacturing to Bloom's specifications — hydraulic pressure testing, dimensional tolerances on brazed manifolds, traceability requirements — upgraded Kaori's process controls in ways that no domestic customer had previously demanded. Plant 3 at the Zhongli campus was completed in 2010–2011 specifically to house the fuel cell hotbox production lines, representing a capital commitment that signaled management's confidence in the partnership's longevity. That confidence was validated: by the Q4 2025 earnings call, Financial VP Wu Jun-Ying reported that fuel cell hotbox revenue to Bloom had grown more than 50% year-over-year, with order visibility described as "quite high, with current production and shipments being intensive." Bloom's own acceleration, driven by data-center power supply contracts, had transformed the fuel cell segment into a secondary AI tailwind independent of Kaori's CDU business.

## China, Scale, and the Geopolitical Parenthesis

Kaori Technology (Ningbo) was established in 2004 as the company's mainland China production beachhead, serving the BPHE demand growing within China's construction and HVAC markets and providing lower-cost manufacturing capacity for volume product lines. A Benzhou production facility followed in 2010–2011, partly to co-locate fuel cell component production closer to Chinese supply chains. The strategy was conventional for a Taiwan industrial company of Kaori's scale: use mainland capacity to serve mainland demand and to compete on cost for export orders where Taiwanese labor costs were disadvantageous.

The geopolitical reconfiguration that began accelerating after 2022 — U.S.-China technology restrictions, supply chain diversification mandates from hyperscaler customers, and the general de-risking of Taiwan-originating supply chains from mainland China exposure — introduced complexity that the company has navigated without public disclosure of any formal China exit. The more telling signal is in Kaori's investment geography: its two announced greenfield facilities — the Zhongli Industrial Park campus targeted for end-2027 completion and the Qiaotou Science Park campus in Kaohsiung targeted for end-2028 — are both on Taiwan. The capital allocation speaks to where management expects its most demanding customers to require production provenance.

## The 2014 Main-Board Listing

Kaori graduated from Taiwan's OTC market to the Taiwan Stock Exchange main board in 2014, a transition that carried symbolic weight beyond the mechanical change of trading venue. Main-board listing on the TWSE imposes stricter disclosure standards, attracts a broader institutional investor base, and signals to customers and partners that a company is of a scale and governance quality commensurate with the demands of major commercial relationships. For a company whose largest customers were already multinational — Bloom Energy, HVAC OEMs in Europe — the listing formalized Kaori's self-positioning as a global industrial supplier rather than a Taoyuan precision-machining workshop.

## From Alibaba to NVIDIA: The AI Thermal Arc

The data-center liquid cooling chapter opens with an engineering partnership that most observers would not have anticipated as a harbinger: in 2018, Kaori's coolant distribution unit systems were subjected to high-pressure validation testing during Alibaba's Double Eleven Shopping Festival, one of the highest-traffic computing events on the calendar. The validation was significant not because Alibaba became a large volume customer but because the testing regime established that Kaori's CDU platform could perform under the sustained thermal and hydraulic loads of hyperscale deployment. It was an engineering proof-of-concept with reputational consequences.

The commercial inflection came with NVIDIA's Blackwell architecture. The GB200 NVL72 rack system — 72 Blackwell GPUs in a single rack, generating thermal densities that air cooling cannot economically address — required a coolant distribution infrastructure built around vacuum-brazed manifolds and headers capable of operating at pressures up to 10 bar with defect rates approaching zero. [Morgan Stanley research](https://www.morganstanley.com/) identified Kaori in 2024 as a key CDU supplier for Supermicro's GB200-based liquid cooling platform, the primary initial deployment vehicle for Blackwell in the hyperscaler buildout. The establishment of Kaori Thermal Technology Co., Ltd. as a dedicated liquid-cooling subsidiary — with its own Dongyuan and Ziqiang factories in Taoyuan, its own brand debut at COMPUTEX 2025, and its own OTC listing preparation underway — was the organizational crystallization of a capability that had been accumulating for decades.

## The Fifty-Five Year Arc

The straight line from 1970 to 2026 is not obvious until you hold both ends simultaneously. H.S. Hans returned from Germany with expertise in controlling metallurgical transformation at elevated temperatures. In 2026, Chairman Allen Wu — who holds a Ph.D. in Materials Science from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and spent years at Motech Industries before bringing advanced materials science into Kaori's R&D — is scaling that same vacuum brazing capability to supply NVIDIA's GB200 thermal infrastructure. The furnaces are more sophisticated. The specifications are set by American engineers again, as they were with Bloom Energy. The quality systems are calibrated to the failure tolerance of hardware running billion-dollar GPU clusters. But the foundational competency — the ability to join metal components in a controlled high-temperature vacuum, to build leak-free thermal assemblies that perform at the edge of material limits — is the same capability that H.S. Hans built in Hsin-Chuan city with NTD 2.6 million and a German education. Fifty-five years of compounding technical specificity have produced a company that the AI data-center buildout needs and cannot easily replicate.

chapters.title: The Product Stack: Brazed Plate Heat Exchangers, Coolant Distribution Units, and SOFC Hotboxes — Three Product Families on One Vacuum-Brazing Platform
chapters.body:
## The Vacuum-Brazing Platform: One Process, Three Markets

Kaori Heat Treatment's product catalogue spans refrigeration chillers, AI data-centre cooling racks, and solid-oxide fuel cell power systems — an apparent breadth that masks a singular manufacturing logic. Every product in the portfolio, from a compact brazed-plate heat exchanger destined for a European heat pump to a coolant distribution unit wired into an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 rack, originates on the same vacuum-brazing production line. Understanding that platform is the prerequisite to understanding why the company is positioned where it is.

Vacuum brazing is a joining process in which metal components are assembled with a filler-metal paste applied at the joint interfaces, then loaded into a sealed furnace from which all oxygen is evacuated before the heating cycle begins. As the furnace reaches brazing temperature — typically 800–1,100 degrees Celsius depending on the base metal and filler system — the filler flows by capillary action through the joint gap, typically 0.05 to 0.15 millimetres, and on cooling forms a metallurgical bond whose tensile strength approaches that of the parent material. The vacuum environment eliminates oxidation at the joint surface, the single largest source of void formation and leak paths in conventionally brazed or welded assemblies. For heat exchangers carrying refrigerants, high-pressure coolants, or process fluids at elevated temperature, the resulting joint integrity is the specification that matters: no voids, no porosity, no flux residue that would degrade downstream system cleanliness.

The capital cost of a production-grade vacuum brazing system — industrial batch or continuous-belt furnaces, associated metrology, inert-atmosphere handling, and the process-control software needed to maintain temperature uniformity within plus or minus three degrees across a loaded work chamber — runs to tens of millions of dollars for a credible throughput capacity. The process knowledge to operate those systems consistently, qualifying joint geometries across dozens of base-metal and filler combinations, takes years to accumulate. For a generic sheet-metal fabricator, the investment horizon and learning curve represent a practical barrier to entry. For Kaori, fifty-five years of continuous metallurgical operation in Taoyuan has produced process libraries, certified operators, and furnace configurations that a new entrant would require a decade to replicate. That accumulated process capital is the company's deepest competitive asset.

## Brazed Plate Heat Exchangers: The Foundational Product Family

The brazed plate heat exchanger was the product that redefined Kaori from an industrial metal-treatment shop into a thermal-product manufacturer when the BPHE division was established in 1994. The defining performance parameter is active heat-transfer area: [Kaori's catalogue](https://www.kaori.com.tw/en) spans from under 0.02 square metres in the smallest single-circuit units to over 3.0 square metres in the largest multi-pass configurations, covering virtually the entire range required by commercial and light-industrial refrigeration, heat pump, HVAC, and process-cooling applications.

The BPHE's physics derive from counter-flow plate geometry: two fluid streams — typically a refrigerant and a secondary coolant — flow on opposite sides of corrugated stainless steel plates in counter-current paths, maximising the mean temperature difference driving heat transfer per unit volume. The vacuum-brazed assembly bonds hundreds of individual plates into a compact block that, at equivalent thermal duty, occupies a fraction of the footprint of a shell-and-tube heat exchanger. For original equipment manufacturers building chillers, heat pumps, and semiconductor process-cooling tools, the size and weight reduction is commercially significant; for applications where operating pressure exceeds 30 bar — high-stage refrigerants, supercritical CO₂ cycles — the joint integrity of vacuum-brazed construction versus gasketed alternatives is non-negotiable from a leak-liability perspective.

Kaori holds CE certification for the European pressure-equipment directive, UL listing for North America, and multiple regional marks that allow direct supply to OEM customers across geographies. The customer base today spans HVAC refrigeration OEMs in Europe and Asia, Taiwanese semiconductor equipment manufacturers, marine engineering applications, electric vehicle battery thermal management integrators in greater China, and utility-scale energy storage systems where waste-heat recovery from battery thermal cycles feeds ORC generation.

## Data-Centre Liquid Cooling: The Growth Engine

The architecture of a liquid-cooled AI compute cluster creates demand for a hierarchy of thermal products, and Kaori — through both the parent company and its dedicated subsidiary [Kaori Thermal Technology](https://www.kaorithermal.com) — now addresses every layer of that hierarchy.

At the rack level, the Coolant Distribution Unit (CDU) is the hydraulic brain of the liquid cooling system. It receives facility-side chilled water, conditions and circulates the secondary coolant loop to the server inlets, monitors supply and return temperatures and flow rates via embedded control software, and manages heat rejection to the facility loop. Kaori supplies two CDU configurations: an **In-Rack CDU** designed to mount within a standard server rack and serve the compute nodes in that rack directly, and an **In-Row CDU** designed for row-level aggregation serving multiple racks from a shared manifold. Both variants carry the vacuum-brazed stainless heat exchanger core that is Kaori's manufacturing signature, and both incorporate proprietary embedded control software for CDU monitoring and alarm management — a capability that hyperscaler procurement teams require for remote fleet management.

For NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72 architecture, Kaori supplies **Coolant Distribution Manifolds (CDMs)** — the plumbing backbone that distributes coolant from a CDU to individual GPU trays within a rack — as well as **MGX Liquid Manifolds** for Intel and AMD reference architectures. The company's products carry qualification for GB200, GB300, and ORV3 open-rack platforms. A **Rear-Door Heat Exchanger** variant captures the exhaust heat from air-cooled servers at the rack door, converting a conventional air-cooled rack to partial liquid cooling without server-level modification; the **SideCar** module performs an analogous function in a side-mounted form factor for retrofits.

For direct-to-chip and immersion deployments, the product line extends to a **D2C cold-plate system** and three immersion cooling bath configurations differentiated by rack density:

| Configuration | Rack Unit | Thermal Capacity | Primary Target Architecture |
|---|---|---|---|
| Single-phase immersion (compact) | 2U | 3 kW | Edge / entry AI |
| Single-phase immersion (mid) | 4U | 7 kW | Standard AI server |
| Single-phase immersion (deep) | 25U | 90 kW | GB200 NVL72 / ORV3 |

The PUE delta versus conventional air cooling is the commercial headline: Kaori's D2C cold-plate system achieves a power usage effectiveness of 1.2, and the full-bath immersion system reaches 1.1, compared to a typical well-engineered air-cooled data centre at 1.3–1.5. For a hyperscaler operating a 100-megawatt campus, that efficiency delta translates directly to hundreds of millions of dollars in annualised energy cost.

The 2018 Alibaba Double Eleven validation — during which Kaori CDU systems underwent high-pressure testing across one of the world's largest simultaneous compute demand events — provided the engineering proof-of-concept that unlocked hyperscaler qualification conversations.

## SOFC Hotboxes: Extending Vacuum Brazing to 800 Degrees

The solid-oxide fuel cell hotbox is, mechanically, among the most demanding precision-fabrication challenges in commercial energy technology. A solid-oxide fuel cell generates electricity through electrochemical oxidation of hydrogen or natural gas across a ceramic electrolyte operating between 700 and 950 degrees Celsius — temperatures that eliminate conventional polymer sealing materials and impose extreme requirements on the metal components that form the structural and thermal architecture of the "hotbox" assembly enclosing the cell stacks.

The hotbox is the insulated high-temperature module at the core of a Bloom Energy Server. It houses the fuel cell stack assemblies, the internal reformer that converts pipeline natural gas to hydrogen-rich synthesis gas, the recuperative heat exchangers that pre-heat incoming air and fuel streams using exhaust heat from the stacks, and the manifolds and seals that distribute these streams at the operating pressure and temperature the electrochemistry demands. Every joint in this assembly must remain leak-free at operating temperature, through thousands of thermal cycles between ambient and operating temperature, and must accommodate differential thermal expansion between dissimilar metals and ceramics in close proximity.

Kaori's 2009 technology-transfer agreement with Bloom Energy brought the company's vacuum-brazing and precision metal-forming competencies directly to bear on this application. The Zhongli Plant 3 dedicated hotbox production line, completed in 2010–2011, represented a manufacturing investment calibrated specifically for the SOFC application. That Bloom Energy — a company with access to global precision manufacturing suppliers — selected and has retained a Taiwanese vacuum-brazing specialist as a critical supply partner speaks to the degree to which SOFC hotbox manufacturing selects for exactly the metallurgical process depth Kaori has accumulated.

Fuel cell hotbox revenue to Bloom Energy grew more than 50% year-over-year in fiscal 2025, a surge that Financial Vice President Wu Jun-Ying attributed on the Q4 2025 earnings call to Bloom's own acceleration in AI data-centre power supply contracts:

> "Order visibility is quite high, with current production and shipments being intensive."

The observation captures the structural logic of Kaori's fuel cell position: as AI data centres seek on-site generation to supplement stressed grid connections, Bloom Energy wins power contracts, and Kaori captures the resulting hotbox volume — a second, independent AI-demand tailwind entirely distinct from the CDU business.

## Vertical Integration as Qualification Currency

Kaori's competitive position in hyperscaler vendor qualification rests on four technical differentiators that the company consistently cites in customer engagement. First, **in-house vacuum brazing of heat exchanger cores** means that Kaori controls the most process-critical and capital-intensive step without subcontractor dependency or inspection risk. Second, **integrated assembly and welding** — stainless headers, manifold welds, pressure-rated port connections — performed on the same campus eliminates inter-site tolerance stack-up. Third, **embedded CDU control software**, developed internally, delivers the monitoring and alarm integration that hyperscaler data-centre management systems require. Fourth, **full in-house hydraulic and thermal testing capability** allows every unit to be pressure-cycled and thermal-performance verified before shipment — a requirement that becomes non-negotiable when a defective CDU failure in a billion-dollar GPU cluster carries catastrophic downstream risk.

Individually, each of these capabilities is replicable. Their combination, executed at high volume with ISO-certified quality systems and validated against GB200 NVL72 rack architecture specifications, represents the kind of integrated supplier profile that a hyperscaler procurement team can qualify once and then scale with confidence.

## Product Roadmap: 2027–2028 and the Greenfield Ramp

Public management commentary and construction timelines provide the outline of what the Kaori product stack could look like by 2028. The Zhongli Industrial Park greenfield campus, targeted for end-2027 completion, is designed to roughly double brazed-core capacity and add dedicated liquid cooling assembly lines. The Qiaotou Science Park facility in Kaohsiung, targeting end-2028, positions Kaori adjacent to TSMC advanced packaging operations and the EMS/ODM cluster in Kaohsiung's industrial belt — a geography increasingly relevant as NVIDIA's Vera Rubin architecture, the successor to Blackwell, enters supply-chain qualification cycles.

Management references to Vera Rubin-compatible architectures in investor commentary suggest the CDU and manifold product line is already being extended to accommodate next-generation rack thermal densities, which analyst projections place above 100 kW per rack for dense GPU configurations. The immersion cooling capacity scale-up — with the 25U/90kW bath system representing the current ceiling — is the product-development vector most likely to extend upward as rack densities escalate. If the two greenfield factories ramp on schedule, Kaori's aggregate brazed-core and liquid-cooling assembly capacity in 2028 could support revenue in excess of two to three times the 2025 base — a capacity addition whose utilisation will depend on whether hyperscaler liquid-cooling adoption continues on the trajectory management has projected: from 18% of new deployments in 2025 toward 57–76% in 2026 and beyond.

The 2021–2022 recovery was conventional industrial-cycle fare: brazed plate heat exchangers (BPHEs) for refrigeration OEMs and industrial process cooling rebounded as pandemic-era supply chains normalised, and Bloom Energy hotbox orders began their slow-burn acceleration. The 2023 step-change — a 52% revenue surge — was qualitatively different. That was the year Kaori converted its first generation of AI data-centre design engagements into commercial revenue: initial coolant distribution unit shipments for hyperscale customers, early manifold orders against NVIDIA's Hopper architecture roadmap, and the beginning of the product-mix shift that would define the company's financial profile.

The 2024 contraction — modest in absolute terms but meaningful as a signal — reflected a pause that was industry-wide rather than company-specific. Hyperscalers absorbed Hopper-generation builds while NVIDIA completed the engineering transition to Blackwell. For Kaori, 2024 was the year of GB200 qualification work: thermal cycling, pressure testing, and supply-chain audits at customer sites that generated engineering costs without proportional revenue. Management acknowledged the trough candidly, framing it as validation investment rather than lost demand.

Then came 2025. The 65% revenue surge to NTD 6.58 billion (~USD 207 million) was not a gradual ramp but a sharp step-function conversion of qualification wins into purchase orders. Monthly TWSE revenue filings told the intra-year story in granular detail: volumes accumulated through the first half, then accelerated materially in the back half as GB200 NVL72 rack deployments scaled at Supermicro's major hyperscaler customers. The Q1 2026 monthly sequence — NTD 642 million in January, NTD 934 million in February, NTD 1.27 billion in March — implies a first-quarter total near NTD 2.85 billion, more than Kaori generated in the entirety of fiscal 2021. The March figure represented approximately 216% year-over-year growth. Against management's [2026 guidance of approximately 80% revenue growth](https://finance.biggo.com/news/TW_8996.TW_2026-03-10), that implies full-year revenue near NTD 11.8 billion (~USD 371 million) — a number the Q1 run-rate appears to validate, and potentially understate.

## Margin Architecture: The CDU Premium and Its Limits

Kaori's gross margin progression is the most revealing financial signal of its product-mix transformation. The company operated in the low-to-mid 20s for years as a predominantly BPHE manufacturer — a category subject to steel-price exposure, annual price negotiations with OEM customers, and limited pricing power relative to larger European plate heat exchanger incumbents. That margin profile was structurally capped.

The CDU business changed the equation. Liquid-cooling hardware for AI data centres commands gross margins substantially above the BPHE baseline, reflecting the precision engineering content, the qualification barriers, the absence of direct commodity competitors at scale, and the criticality of the product to billion-dollar GPU cluster deployments where downtime costs are measured in millions per hour. As CDU revenue scaled from roughly 20% of the total in FY2024 to approximately 35% in FY2025, consolidated gross margin expanded from the mid-20s toward a peak of approximately 33% in at least one FY2025 quarter.

The Q4 2025 pullback to 27.3% introduced an important caveat. Product mix within the CDU category is not uniform: in-rack CDU systems for NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 deployments carry the highest margins; manifold components and rear-door heat exchangers are more commoditised. When shipment schedules weight toward manifolds and away from full CDU systems — as appears to have occurred in Q4 2025 — consolidated margin compresses even as top-line revenue holds. The implication for margin forecasting is that the 33% peak should be understood as a high-mix outcome rather than a structural floor.

The forward margin trajectory depends on two competing forces. On the expansion side: management has guided liquid cooling toward 50% of total 2026 revenue (versus 35% in FY2025), the two greenfield factories will eventually absorb fixed overhead across a larger revenue base, and CDU pricing per rack unit has been sticky as GB300 and Vera Rubin roadmaps layer additional thermal demands. On the compression side: the greenfield factories will begin carrying depreciation charges before they achieve utilisation rates sufficient to offset them, and as more competitors complete qualification programs through 2026–2027, pricing pressure on manifold and secondary components is probable. The net result is likely a margin corridor of 28–32% through the medium term, with quarterly volatility driven by delivery mix.

## Earnings, Dividends, and the Payout Calculus

Kaori's FY2025 net income reached approximately NTD 829 million (~USD 26 million), a roughly 40% year-over-year increase on 65% revenue growth — a relationship that reflects operating leverage partially offset by rising staff and R&D costs as the company built out the engineering teams required to support GB200 and GB300 qualification pipelines. On approximately 91.98 million diluted shares, that produced diluted EPS of approximately [NTD 8.90](https://stockanalysis.com/quote/tpe/8996/), and EBITDA of approximately NTD 1.22 billion (~USD 38 million) at an 18.5% EBITDA margin.

The board declared a dividend of NTD 4.56 per share for FY2025, maintaining a roughly 50% payout ratio that has been a consistent feature of Kaori's capital return policy. At the prevailing share price range, that implies a yield of approximately 0.4–0.8% — modest by dividend-stock standards but consistent with Taiwan's retail shareholder culture, which treats dividend continuity as a proxy for management confidence. Given the dual-factory construction program absorbing capital through 2026–2028, the board faces an emerging tension: whether to sustain the 50% payout or redirect a larger fraction of free cash flow toward CapEx. As of the frozen snapshot, no change in dividend policy had been signalled.

Q1 2026 run-rates suggest full-year 2026 EPS well above the NTD 8.90 FY2025 base, with analyst consensus price targets near [NTD 1,385](https://stockanalysis.com/quote/tpe/8996/) implying embedded forward EPS estimates in the NTD 15–18 range — a forward growth assumption broadly consistent with the 80% revenue guidance if operating leverage delivers incremental margin conversion.

## Valuation: What 79x Trailing P/E Requires

At trailing earnings of NTD 8.90 and a share price near the 52-week high, Kaori's trailing P/E of approximately 79x places it in the rarefied tier of Taiwanese industrial equities priced for transformational growth rather than cyclical recovery. The forward P/E of approximately 49x implies the market is already underwriting a roughly 60% EPS increase in fiscal 2026 — a demanding hurdle that Q1 2026 monthly revenue data suggests is achievable but not certain to be exceeded.

| Company | Ticker | Market Cap (USD B) | NTM P/E (approx.) | NTM EV/EBITDA (approx.) | Growth Profile |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kaori Heat Treatment | 8996.TW | ~3.5 | ~49x | ~35x | AI liquid cooling; 80% guided revenue growth |
| Vertiv Holdings | VRT (NYSE) | ~50 | ~35x | ~25x | Data-centre thermal/power; 15–20% growth |
| Modine Manufacturing | MOD (NYSE) | ~3–4 | ~22x | ~14x | Data-centre cooling; 20–25% growth |
| nVent Electric | NVT (NYSE) | ~10 | ~20x | ~16x | Precision cooling/enclosures; 8–12% growth |

The Kaori multiple premium over even the most growth-oriented peers reflects three embedded assumptions: first, that liquid-cooling adoption in AI data centres will continue to accelerate from an estimated 18% of new deployments in 2025 toward 57–76% by 2026–2027, as thermal density mandates associated with GB300 and Vera Rubin architectures make air-cooling uneconomical; second, that Kaori retains its qualification position as the dominant CDU supplier for Supermicro's NVIDIA Blackwell builds; and third, that the Kaori Thermal Technology OTC listing, if completed, provides a valuation event that crystallises the liquid-cooling business's standalone worth at a premium to the consolidated entity. All three assumptions require continued execution. The Q1 2026 monthly trajectory is consistent with the first two; the listing timeline remains management-dependent.

## The CapEx Imperative: Funding Two Greenfields

Kaori entered its current expansion cycle in a financially comfortable position. FY2025 CapEx of approximately NTD 300 million (~USD 9.4 million) represented just 24.6% of EBITDA — a modest capital intensity ratio that left substantial free cash flow for dividends and debt service. The company generated free cash flow materially above its dividend obligation, supporting the balance sheet entering the construction phase.

The construction program shifts that calculus substantially. The Zhongli Industrial Park greenfield — targeted for completion by end-2027 — and the Qiaotou Science Park campus in Kaohsiung — targeted end-2028 to early-2029 — represent a step-change in capital requirements. Based on management commentary referencing syndicated bank facilities alongside operating cash as funding sources, the aggregate construction cost of the two facilities likely runs into the NTD 2–3 billion range over three to four years (~USD 63–94 million), with the peak drawdown period coinciding with 2026–2027. Against guided 2026 revenue of NTD 11.8 billion at roughly 18–19% EBITDA margin, the company would generate approximately NTD 2.1–2.2 billion in annual EBITDA — sufficient to self-fund the construction program over its duration if margins hold, with residual capacity for dividend maintenance at the existing payout ratio. The critical variable is whether greenfield depreciation, which will front-load before new capacity fills, creates a margin headwind that compresses EBITDA below that threshold in 2027–2028.

Management has flagged syndicated loan facilities as a potential supplement without disclosing committed facilities as of the frozen snapshot. No convertible bond or equity issuance has been announced. Debt-to-equity remains relatively modest by the standards of Taiwanese industrial infrastructure peers, and covenant risk appears low given the company's demonstrated cash generation capacity.

## Balance Sheet and the Subsidiary Listing Variable

From the most recent quarterly filings available as of the frozen snapshot, Kaori's balance sheet reflects a net-positive liquidity position: cash and short-term investments exceed outstanding bank debt, producing a net cash or near-neutral net debt condition. The company enters its capital-intensive phase without the burden of legacy leverage, which materially reduces refinancing and covenant risk even as bank debt climbs through 2026–2028.

The more structurally complex element is the planned OTC listing of Kaori Thermal Technology on the Taipei Exchange. The subsidiary concentrates all OEM and DFM services for AI data-centre clients and operates the Dongyuan and Ziqiang factories that are the operational core of the CDU business. Kaori has stated an intent to retain at least 55% post-listing, which preserves consolidation and operational control. The listing, if executed at a premium to the parent's implied CDU valuation, would provide three potential benefits: it monetises the liquid-cooling franchise for minority shareholders, creates a publicly traded currency for subsidiary-level acquisitions or partnerships, and establishes a market reference price that could serve as a floor for the parent's own valuation. The complication is that listing the subsidiary at a high multiple could simultaneously highlight the discount embedded in the parent's consolidated valuation — drawing activist attention — and create inter-company transfer pricing and related-party governance scrutiny from the Financial Supervisory Commission.

## Financial Risk: Operating Leverage, Concentration, and the Dilution Question

Three financial risks warrant explicit pricing. The first is revenue concentration: by management's own guidance, liquid-cooling revenue will represent approximately 50% of the 2026 total. Any deceleration in hyperscaler CDU procurement — whether from capex pauses, architectural shifts, or supply-chain diversification by key customers — would remove the highest-margin, highest-growth segment from the revenue base simultaneously, compressing both top-line and margin, and likely triggering multiple compression disproportionate to the underlying cash flow impact given the current premium P/E.

The second risk is operating leverage in its most consequential form. Two greenfield factories with combined capital requirements likely exceeding NTD 2 billion will carry fixed depreciation and staffing costs beginning before their utilisation curves justify them. A revenue shortfall against the NTD 11.8 billion 2026 guidance in any quarter would expose fixed-cost absorption ratios that the current earnings model does not fully price, translating a modest revenue miss into a material EPS disappointment.

The third risk is dilution. While no equity raise has been announced as of the frozen snapshot, the combination of greenfield CapEx requirements, a potential subsidiary listing, and the leverage implications of syndicated facilities leave open the possibility that Kaori's capital structure evolves in ways that dilute existing shareholders' claims on the operating earnings of either the parent or the liquid-cooling subsidiary. The market, pricing Kaori at approximately 79x trailing earnings, has assumed none of that dilution. The financial anatomy described in this chapter — a company with genuine competitive advantage in vacuum-brazed thermal management, executing a well-timed pivot into AI data-centre infrastructure — is robust. What is less certain is whether the earnings multiple at which the market has priced that anatomy leaves room for the construction detours, mix volatility, and capital structure evolution that multi-year industrial transformations invariably produce.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
By the frozen snapshot of 23 May 2026, Taiwan's investment community had bestowed on Kaori Heat Treatment a valuation that sits well outside the comfort zone of any industrial-peer screening tool. A trailing price-to-earnings multiple of approximately 79 times FY2025 diluted earnings per share of NTD 8.90, and a forward multiple of approximately 49 times consensus FY2026 estimates, places the Taoyuan manufacturer in the company of growth technology businesses rather than heat-exchanger fabricators — a classification shift that is partly justified by the underlying facts and partly a reflection of narrative premium with a well-documented history of being painful to unwind.

The share price, which touched a 52-week high of NTD 1,310 before settling toward levels consistent with those trailing multiples, produced a market capitalisation that, at its apex, reached approximately NTD 111–112 billion — roughly USD 3.5 billion at prevailing exchange rates of approximately 31.8 TWD per dollar — on 91.98 million shares outstanding. [Source: [Kaori Heat Treatment IR / TWSE](https://www.kaori.com.tw/en/modules/investors/annualreports)] The 52-week trough was NTD 232. The stock has already more than repaid early-2025 bulls. What matters now is whether the residual premium makes sense at this stage of the AI-cycle.

## Current Multiples and Their Anatomy

The trailing 79x multiple reflects FY2025 net income of approximately NTD 829 million on revenue of NTD 6.58 billion — a net margin of 12.6% that represents a meaningful step up from prior-year levels but remains depressed by Kaori's front-loaded capital deployment ahead of two greenfield factory completions. [Source: [StockAnalysis / Kaori FY2025 data](https://stockanalysis.com/quote/tpe/8996/)] EBITDA reached approximately NTD 1.22 billion, an 18.5% EBITDA margin, implying an enterprise-value-to-EBITDA ratio in the low-to-mid 50s times at the prevailing market capitalisation once modest net debt is added to equity value — a figure that assumes the balance sheet remains conservatively geared, as management has indicated heading into the greenfield CapEx cycle.

On a price-to-sales basis, the stock trades at approximately 10 times trailing FY2025 revenue. That ratio compresses sharply when applied against management's own 2026 guidance of approximately 80% revenue growth, which would carry the top line to roughly NTD 11.8 billion. Against that forward revenue, the EV/Sales ratio falls toward 5–6 times — broadly in line with the upper end of the global data-centre thermal-infrastructure peer set but still carrying a premium to lower-growth industrial comparables. The PEG ratio, applying the 79x trailing P/E against FY2025 net-income growth of approximately 40% year-over-year, yields a reading near 2.0 — elevated by value-investor standards but arguably defensible given the documented revenue acceleration through Q1 2026.

## Historical Re-Rating: From Industrial to Infrastructure

Kaori carried a single-digit-to-low-teens P/E as recently as 2021–2022. Prior to the AI liquid-cooling thesis crystallising in late 2023 and accelerating through the GB200 ramp of 2024–2025, the stock traded at multiples consistent with a Taiwanese precision-components business serving HVAC and fuel-cell customers: roughly 12–18 times earnings, with occasional peaks during periods of BPHE demand strength. [Source: [Macrotrends historical revenue / price data](https://www.macrotrends.net/stocks/charts/8996.TW/kaori-heat/revenue)] The re-rating from that baseline to 79 times trailing earnings represents a roughly four- to six-fold multiple expansion, layered atop revenue and earnings growth that would have been considered extraordinary in the company's pre-AI era.

The critical question is whether this is a durable re-rating — reflecting a permanent shift in the quality and duration of the earnings stream — or narrative inflation that arrived ahead of the underlying earnings power. The honest answer, as of the frozen snapshot, is that both are partially true, and the balance between them will be settled by the 2026–2027 results cycle.

## Peer Comparison

The most instructive peer set spans global data-centre thermal management and the Taiwanese AI supply chain. Figures below are approximate, based on publicly available market data near the frozen snapshot; they are directional rather than audited.

| Company | Ticker | Approx. Mkt Cap | Trailing P/E | Fwd P/E | EV/EBITDA | Est. Rev. Growth |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kaori Heat Treatment | 8996.TW | USD ~2–3.5B | ~79x | ~49x | ~50–55x | ~80% (2026E) |
| Vertiv Holdings | VRT | ~USD 50B | ~65x | ~35x | ~38x | ~20–25% |
| Modine Manufacturing | MOD | ~USD 3–4B | ~28x | ~22x | ~18x | ~15–20% |
| nVent Electric | NVT | ~USD 10B | ~22x | ~19x | ~15x | ~10–12% |
| AcBel Polytech | 6277.TW | ~USD 1–2B | ~35x | ~25x | ~18–20x | ~30–40% |
| Asetek | ASETEK.OL | ~USD 0.3B | NM | ~28x | ~22x | ~20–25% |

The table makes Kaori's growth-rate premium legible: at a projected 80% revenue expansion in 2026, no named peer approaches the top-line velocity. Vertiv — the most natural large-cap comparable, with deep data-centre thermal exposure and a USD 50 billion market capitalisation — trades at roughly half Kaori's trailing multiple while growing at roughly one-quarter the pace. Modine Manufacturing, which has successfully pivoted its own data-centre cooling segment, carries a far more modest multiple on materially slower growth. AcBel Polytech, which shares Kaori's Bloom Energy hotbox exposure and Taiwanese supply-chain DNA, trades at a meaningful discount, plausibly reflecting its less-developed CDU portfolio and the absence of an OTC spin-out catalyst. The gap between Kaori and its closest peer on growth metrics is wide enough to support a structural premium. The question is whether 49–79 times captures that premium appropriately or overshoots.

## What the Multiple Implies: A DCF Frame

A back-of-envelope discounted cash flow against the market capitalisation range reveals the assumptions embedded in the current price. Working with a 12% WACC — reflecting Taiwan equity risk premium, currency exposure inherent in a USD-revenue business with TWD cost structures, and AI-cycle duration uncertainty — and a 3% terminal growth rate, the prevailing capitalisation requires free cash flow growing at approximately 30–35% annually for seven years before normalisation, followed by a decade of single-digit expansion. That trajectory is not implausible given the greenfield factories' capacity additions, the secular liquid-cooling adoption curve, and management's demonstrated ability to win qualification slots at NVIDIA Blackwell-architecture customers.

What the DCF does not tolerate is a pause. A two-year period of flat free cash flow — plausible if both greenfield facilities come online amid a temporary hyperscaler CapEx digestion cycle — degrades the intrinsic-value estimate by approximately 25–35%, depending on the assumed recovery rate. The margin of safety against a pause scenario is thin.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — NTD 1,300–1,400:** FY2026 revenue reaches NTD 12.5–13.0 billion, modestly ahead of the 80% growth guidance, as CDU and manifold shipments to GB300 and ORV3 platforms ramp through the second half of the year. Gross margins recover toward 31–33% on favourable product mix and operating leverage. Net income reaches NTD 2.0–2.2 billion, delivering EPS of approximately NTD 22–24. The market awards 58–60 times forward earnings as the Kaori Thermal Technology OTC listing crystallises a sum-of-parts premium and provides an independent valuation anchor for the liquid-cooling subsidiary. Price target converges on the analyst consensus of approximately NTD 1,385. [Source: [Kaori consensus data, StockAnalysis](https://stockanalysis.com/quote/tpe/8996/)]

**Base case — NTD 750–950:** FY2026 revenue comes in at NTD 10.5–11.5 billion, achieving the guided growth rate, but margin pressure from greenfield depreciation and a softer-than-hoped product mix keeps net income in the NTD 1.3–1.6 billion range — EPS of approximately NTD 14–17. The multiple settles in the 50–55x range as institutional investors continue to treat Kaori as the most liquid Taiwan AI-cooling proxy. The Kaori Thermal Technology listing provides a mild re-rating catalyst if executed cleanly, partially offsetting CapEx drag.

**Bear case — NTD 280–420:** A pronounced pause in hyperscaled liquid-cooled deployment — driven by hyperscaler CapEx cuts, an NVIDIA architecture shift toward improved air-cooling tolerance, or displacement by a larger ODM competitor with deeper balance-sheet resources — reduces 2026 revenue to NTD 8.5–9.5 billion. Net margins compress to 9–10% as fixed factory costs spread over lower volumes. EPS falls back toward NTD 8–10. The multiple re-rates sharply toward 25–35 times as growth-premium justification evaporates. Shares retrace toward NTD 280–350 — territory last visited in mid-2025 before the GB200 ramp lit the chart.

## Consensus vs. The Dossier's Read

The analyst consensus price target of approximately NTD 1,385 as of the frozen snapshot implies that the buy-side's central scenario is essentially this dossier's bull case. The market is pricing in execution of management's 2026 guidance as a near-certainty, the Kaori Thermal Technology OTC listing as a free embedded option, and a multi-year liquid-cooling adoption curve sustaining 30%+ revenue growth through at least 2028.

This dossier's read diverges on one specific dimension: the market is under-pricing the CapEx transition risk in 2027–2028, when both greenfield factories will simultaneously draw on operating cash and bank facilities while carrying front-loaded depreciation that will depress reported earnings regardless of the revenue trajectory. The dual-factory build creates a roughly 24-month window — the second half of 2027 through 2028 — in which Kaori's P&L will look optically worse than the underlying business quality warrants. A retail-heavy, narrative-driven shareholder base conditioned by a 390–498% one-year total return could respond to that optical deterioration disproportionately to any actual business deterioration.

Against that medium-term risk, the near-term revenue data provides genuine cover. Monthly TWSE filings showed NTD 642 million in January 2026, NTD 934 million in February, and NTD 1.27 billion in March — the last figure representing 216% year-over-year growth. [Source: [Finance BigGo / Kaori Q4 FY2025 earnings summary](https://finance.biggo.com/news/TW_8996.TW_2026-03-10)] The question is not whether 2026 delivers; the Q1 trajectory strongly suggests it will. The question is whether the market is building in a 2027–2028 bridge that management will need to earn its way across — in a more demanding capital environment, against a more competitive CDU supplier landscape, and with two unproven factories still ramping to capacity utilisation.

chapters.title: Quarter by Quarter: How Kaori's Management Narrated the AI Inflection from First Pilot Orders to Full Capacity Ramp
chapters.body:
## The Language of Inflection

For the analyst trying to understand when Kaori Heat Treatment's management team genuinely believed it had crossed into a new business — not merely harvesting a cyclical tailwind but standing at the edge of a structural revenue transformation — the company's quarterly earnings commentary provides a remarkably precise record. Read chronologically, from the guarded language of early 2024 through the confident quantitative guidance issued on the Q4 FY2025 call in March 2026, the transcripts trace an arc that mirrors the company's financial metamorphosis almost word for word.

The inflection, it turns out, was not a single moment. It was a sequence of quarterly recalibrations in which management's language tightened and its targets grew more specific as order-book evidence accumulated.

## FY2024: The Pause That Required an Explanation

The revenue contraction from NTD 4.33 billion in FY2023 to NTD 4.00 billion in FY2024 was, by the standards of a company being marketed as Taiwan's purest liquid-cooling proxy trade, an awkward result. Management's task on the earnings calls of that year was to explain a decline without undermining the growth thesis.

The explanation had three components, each of which was credible individually and together constituted a coherent account: the data-center cooling business was real but had not yet converted pilot and qualification work into volume shipments; Bloom Energy — the second pillar of the revenue base — was working through an inventory normalization cycle following the surge in SOFC hotbox demand during 2022 and 2023; and the legacy BPHE segment serving HVAC and refrigeration OEMs was absorbing a global softening in commercial construction. None of these explanations required management to revise the structural thesis.

The liquid cooling revenue mix in FY2024 is estimated at approximately 20% of total revenue — a contribution material enough to be described in quarterly commentary as an "emerging opportunity in data-center cooling" but not yet large enough to anchor full-year guidance to specific growth targets. The language of the period was characteristically hedged: references to qualification pipelines, ongoing engineering engagements with hyperscale clients, and the long validation timelines inherent to mission-critical server infrastructure. Whether the 2024 dip reflected GB200 qualification timing or Bloom inventory normalization — the two most plausible explanations — would only become clear in retrospect, when the 2025 volume ramp vindicated the qualification-timing narrative.

## FY2025: When Specificity Replaced Caution

The shift in management's rhetorical register became audible by mid-2025. Where FY2024 commentary had spoken of "opportunities" and "pipeline development," the quarters of FY2025 introduced the vocabulary of confirmed volume: specific customer platform mentions, references to production intensity, and — for the first time — explicit segment-revenue percentage guidance. Gross margins reaching a peak of approximately 33% in at least one quarter of FY2025 provided the financial data to match the narrative shift. Liquid cooling had become the margin story, not just the growth story.

The full-year FY2025 result of NTD 6.58 billion — a 64.5% increase from the prior year — validated the timing explanation management had offered during the 2024 contraction. Net income reached approximately NTD 829 million, diluted EPS of approximately NTD 8.90, and EBITDA of approximately NTD 1.22 billion at an 18.5% margin. The company declared a dividend of NTD 4.56 per share, sustaining its roughly 50% payout ratio even as the dual-factory greenfield program was simultaneously consuming capital.

The segment mix told the underlying story: liquid cooling reached approximately 35% of FY2025 revenue, up from roughly 20% in FY2024 and from a negligible base two years prior. The BPHE legacy business held its ground. Fuel cells — independent beneficiaries of Bloom Energy's own AI-driven tailwind — grew more than 50% year-over-year as Bloom won data-center power supply contracts that pulled Kaori hotbox orders with them.

## The Q4 FY2025 Earnings Call: Wu Jun-Ying's Clearest Statement

The March 10, 2026 earnings call, covering Q4 FY2025 results, produced the most precise public guidance Kaori's management had yet issued. Financial Vice President Wu Jun-Ying was unambiguous on the fuel cell order trajectory:

> "Order visibility is quite high, with current production and shipments being intensive."

The choice of language — "order visibility is quite high" — is significant precisely because of its departure from the hedged register of prior periods. In Taiwanese mid-cap IR, "high visibility" typically signals twelve-to-eighteen months of confirmed purchase orders or rolling blanket agreements with limited cancellation risk. Combined with "production and shipments being intensive," the statement implied that Bloom Energy's procurement cycle had normalized and was accelerating into 2026.

On liquid cooling, Wu Jun-Ying articulated what analysts had been modeling from channel checks but management had not previously stated as formal guidance: liquid cooling was targeted to reach approximately 50% of total company revenue in 2026, compared to roughly 35% in FY2025. This guidance, set against the company's separate 2026 full-year revenue target implying approximately 80% growth — which would translate to approximately NTD 11.8 billion in full-year revenue — implied that the liquid cooling segment alone was being guided to approximately NTD 5.9 billion, a volume that would represent more than the company's entire revenue as recently as FY2022.

Capital expenditure plans disclosed on the same call reflected the operational confidence: funding for the Zhongli Industrial Park greenfield — targeted for end-2027 completion — and preliminary commitments toward the Qiaotou Science Park campus in Kaohsiung were confirmed as on track, financed through operating cash flow supplemented by bank facilities and the potential for syndicated loan arrangements as the investment cycle deepened into 2027–2028.

## The Monthly Revenue Filings: Ground Truth

Taiwan Stock Exchange disclosure rules require monthly revenue filings, and for a company growing as quickly as Kaori, those filings became in early 2026 the most watched data series in the company's investor relations calendar.

| Month | Revenue (NTD) | YoY Growth |
|-------|--------------|------------|
| January 2026 | 642 million | — |
| February 2026 | 933.8 million | +205.7% |
| March 2026 | ~1.27 billion | ~+216% |

The sequential acceleration across Q1 2026 carried several implications. First, the February and March year-over-year rates — both above 200% — were not aberrations produced by easy prior-year comparables alone; February and March 2025 were themselves strong months in a year that finished at NTD 6.58 billion. Second, the March run-rate of approximately NTD 1.27 billion annualizes to approximately NTD 15 billion — well above the NTD 11.8 billion implied by management's 80% growth guidance, suggesting either that guidance was conservative, that Q1 2026 benefited from shipment timing that would not sustain linearly, or both. Third, the monthly progression from NTD 642 million to NTD 1.27 billion over a single quarter demonstrated that Kaori's order book was not only large but was converting to recognized revenue at an accelerating rate consistent with full production ramp at Kaori Thermal Technology's Dongyuan and Ziqiang facilities.

## Assessing the Quality of Management Communication

The question of whether Wu Jun-Ying's earnings commentary is specific enough to be useful for financial modeling admits a nuanced answer. By the standards of Taiwan's mid-cap industrial IR community — where guidance is frequently limited to vague directional qualifiers and quantitative targets are rare — Kaori's Q4 FY2025 call was unusually informative. The explicit 50% liquid-cooling revenue mix target, the "high visibility" language on fuel cells, and the confirmation of CapEx timing provided three anchor points that a sophisticated financial model could actually use.

The caveat is that these anchors were offered without margin specificity by segment or explicit quarterly cadence. Wu Jun-Ying confirmed the direction and approximate magnitude of the liquid cooling shift but declined — as is standard practice in Taiwanese manufacturing IR — to provide segment-level gross margin guidance or SKU-level volume commitments. The quarter-on-quarter pullback in blended gross margin from approximately 33% at the FY2025 peak to approximately 27.3% in Q4 FY2025 was not fully anticipated in earlier commentary, suggesting that product mix shifts within the liquid cooling segment itself — between CDU units at different margin tiers and manifold components at others — introduce variability that guidance-based models will struggle to capture.

The more significant validation of management's communication credibility lies in the correspondence between the 2024 qualitative narrative — that the revenue dip was transitional, not structural — and the 2025 outcome. Management said the pause was a qualification-timing phenomenon; the 64% revenue surge in FY2025 confirmed it. That alignment between narrative and subsequent result is, ultimately, the most meaningful test of an IR function's reliability as a forecasting tool.

chapters.title: The Builder and the Engineer: Chairman Allen Wu's Materials-Science Edge and the Leadership Team Executing the Liquid Cooling Pivot
chapters.body:
## A Scientist in the Chairman's Seat

The intellectual pedigree of Allen C.H. Wu is not incidental to Kaori Heat Treatment's competitive position — it is, in a meaningful sense, the position itself. Wu holds a doctorate in Materials Science and Engineering from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, one of the world's pre-eminent programmes in the physical metallurgy of metals and ceramics, before joining Motech Industries as Senior Vice President. At Motech, Wu operated inside a company whose commercial logic turned entirely on controlling solid-state transformations at extreme temperatures: the Czochralski process for pulling monocrystalline silicon boules is, at its core, an exercise in managing phase boundaries, dopant diffusion, and thermal gradients across a solidifying crystal lattice. The vocabulary — diffusion coefficients, interface energies, grain boundary chemistry — is precisely the vocabulary that governs what happens when copper and stainless steel are held at 1,100°C in a vacuum furnace and bonded atom-by-atom across a brazed filler interface.

This is not a generic career trajectory from industrial executive to industrial chairman. It is a technically coherent one. The core engineering challenge in Kaori's vacuum-brazed Coolant Distribution Units — achieving leak-free bonds at copper-to-stainless interfaces under operating pressures up to 10 bar while sustaining thermal cycling over tens of thousands of hours — sits squarely within the domain of materials-phase-transformation research. Wu's arrival in Kaori's senior leadership, and his subsequent elevation to Chairman, brought a scientist's understanding of the brazing process to the strategic decisions shaping the company's AI pivot. When Kaori elected to pursue CDU qualification for NVIDIA's GB200 architecture rather than licensing its BPHE designs to a systems integrator, that choice reflected a conviction — intellectually grounded — that the manufacturing process itself was the defensible asset.

Wu has been publicly reticent in the manner common among Taiwanese industrial executives, granting few extended English-language interviews. Commonwealth Magazine, profiling the AI cooling supply chain in 2024, credited Kaori as a central figure in "[driving] Nvidia GB200 liquid cooling" from Taiwan's industrial base — a characterisation that positions Wu's technical decisions in a geopolitically legible frame. His public statements through the company's investor relations channel have been measured and forward-looking, consistently emphasising the durability of the process capability over the specifics of individual product cycles.

## The Operational Counterpart

If Wu occupies the technology-strategy axis of Kaori's leadership dyad, General Manager and Director Leo H.W. Wang (王信武) occupies the operational one with equal rigour. Wang's training at National Central University's Institute of Financial Management — a programme that produces executives with fluency in both manufacturing operations and capital allocation — positioned him as a natural complement to a Chairman whose strengths lie in materials science rather than supply-chain logistics. Wang joined Kaori in an operational capacity and was formally designated Deputy General Manager in January 2006, a tenure that means he was present for the Bloom Energy technology-transfer agreement in 2009, the Alibaba CDU validation in 2018, and every capacity investment cycle in between. His elevation to General Manager and Director, formalised approximately in 2023, consolidated operational authority at a critical moment: Kaori was transitioning from a modestly growing BPHE business into a company managing explosive AI-driven demand while simultaneously constructing two greenfield facilities and preparing a subsidiary for an independent listing.

The division of labour between Wu and Wang follows a pattern common in Taiwanese manufacturing companies that have successfully navigated technology transitions: the Chairman sets the external positioning and technical roadmap, interfaces with strategic partners — Bloom Energy, NVIDIA's ODM ecosystem, hyperscaler procurement teams — and owns the company's intellectual identity; the General Manager runs the factory system, manages the production schedule, and delivers customer commitments. The arrangement is legible in the company's public communications: Wu's voice appears in strategic announcements and Computex-style industry positioning; Wang's authority is visible in the operational cadence and capacity execution.

## Institutional Memory: The Vice Chairman's Role

H.F. Han (韓漢富), who holds the title of Vice Chairman and carries a mechanical engineering background from Tatung University, represents something rarer than technical competence in Kaori's governance structure: uninterrupted institutional memory across the company's entire modern arc. Han has served as General Manager since June 2000 — meaning he was in operating command when Kaori signed the Bloom Energy technology-transfer agreement, when the first CDU prototypes were assembled for Alibaba's validation programme, and when the company made the strategic decision to build a dedicated liquid-cooling subsidiary rather than integrate the business into the parent's BPHE production lines. His transition from General Manager to Vice Chairman, concurrent with Wang's elevation to GM, is a canonical Taiwanese succession pattern: the founding-era executive rotates into a governance oversight role while a professionally trained successor takes operating responsibility.

The [2024 annual report](https://www.kaori.com.tw/tw/uploads/filelist/1000/2/1747120037_dc80eed7efa55933.pdf) — published in Chinese and not fully rendered in English financial media — is the authoritative source for Han's current formal governance responsibilities, including any audit or compensation committee participation. What the public record confirms unambiguously is that his Tatung University mechanical engineering training and his two-decade tenure as General Manager give him firsthand knowledge of the manufacturing decisions that differentiate Kaori's brazing process from potential competitors: the furnace cycle parameters, the flux chemistries, the fixture tolerances that determine bond quality at scale. That knowledge, whether formalised in documented procedures or retained as tacit engineering judgement, is an institutional asset of material strategic value.

## The Newer Layer: Capital-Markets Sophistication

The two most recent named additions to Kaori's executive roster signal a deliberate expansion of the company's capability set in a direction that the founding generation did not require. Chief Strategy Officer Alan H.X. Huang, trained in Technology Management at National Tsing Hua University and previously employed at International Bills Finance Corporation, brings a background that is unusual for an industrial CSO: bills finance in Taiwan operates at the intersection of short-term capital markets, credit structuring, and corporate treasury — competencies that map onto the capital-markets complexity introduced by the Kaori Thermal Technology OTC listing preparation. Preparing a subsidiary for independent listing on the Taipei Exchange requires structuring the entity's balance sheet, managing related-party transaction disclosures, coordinating with underwriters, and building an investor relations infrastructure distinct from the parent. Huang's hiring suggests that management identified this gap and filled it with deliberate intent.

Vice President Gilbert C.Y. Wu (no disclosed relation to the Chairman) brings a Tulane University law degree and an IMD EMBA alongside prior experience at Yuan Tsun Plastic, a Taiwanese industrial company. The combination of legal credentials and an international business school programme is characteristic of executives who manage cross-border contracts, customer qualification processes, and supplier agreements — functions that have grown substantially in complexity as Kaori's CDU customer base has expanded to include U.S. cloud hyperscalers with demanding procurement legal frameworks.

## Founder Succession and Governance Architecture

The company's origin in 1970 under H.S. Hans — a Taiwanese engineer who pursued graduate studies in Germany and returned with expertise in industrial heat treatment metallurgy — established a technical culture that has proved surprisingly durable. Hans founded Kaori with NTD 2.6 million in registered capital and an initial focus on metal heat treatment for Taiwanese manufacturers; the materials-science competency he embedded persists, fifty-five years later, as the technical backbone of the company's vacuum-brazed CDU product line. The details of the transition from Hans to the current management structure are not fully documented in English-language disclosures, and the ownership concentration data for the founding family — potentially visible in TWSE ten-largest-shareholder filings — has not been confirmed in the sources available at the frozen snapshot date. In a Taiwanese family industrial company of Kaori's profile, founder-era ownership concentration is common and typically represents governance continuity rather than governance risk, provided the succeeding management team has sufficient operational authority.

Board composition, as required by TWSE listing rules for companies above applicable market-capitalisation thresholds, includes independent directors. The [2024 annual report](https://www.kaori.com.tw/tw/uploads/filelist/1000/2/1747120037_dc80eed7efa55933.pdf) contains the formal board composition table and independent director disclosures, though granular director-independence data and compensation benchmarking are among the standard disclosure gaps in TWSE small-cap governance filings. A notable structural question — not answered in publicly available sources — is whether any independent director carries deep data-centre technology expertise. At a moment when Kaori's valuation rests substantially on its AI liquid-cooling execution, a board audit committee equipped primarily with general industrial or financial expertise faces a meaningful information asymmetry relative to management on the technical risks of the CDU product roadmap.

## The Unnamed Risk

The most consequential succession risk at Kaori is not named in any executive biography or board resolution. The company's technical differentiation is embedded in its vacuum-brazing process engineering — in the specific furnace programmes, fixture designs, and quality-inspection protocols developed over decades by production engineers whose names do not appear in investor presentations or earnings call transcripts. Chairman Wu's materials-science doctorate and Vice Chairman Han's mechanical engineering background provide named custodians of the intellectual framework. But the translation of that framework into repeatable manufacturing outcomes at the scale demanded by hyperscale CDU orders depends on an institutional knowledge base that resides, in part, on the factory floor in Zhongli.

As Kaori scales from a NTD 6.58 billion revenue business toward the NTD 10-plus billion trajectory implied by its 2026 guidance, and as the two greenfield facilities in Zhongli Industrial Park and Qiaotou Science Park bring new production capacity online by 2027–2028, the central institutional challenge is not executive succession but knowledge transfer: whether the process engineering competencies that differentiate Kaori's brazed cores from competitors' can be codified, taught, and deployed by a substantially larger workforce without degradation. Financial VP Wu Jun-Ying, the company's primary earnings-call voice, has not been quoted on this question directly. It is the question that management has not yet had to answer at scale — and the one that will define whether Kaori's materials-science edge is a durable moat or a constraint on the very growth it has made possible.

chapters.title: Three Customer Ecosystems: The Hyperscaler Demand Pull, Bloom Energy's Fuel Cell Buildout, and the Durable BPHE Industrial Base
chapters.body:
## The Hyperscaler Demand Pull

Kaori Heat Treatment occupies an unusual commercial position in the AI infrastructure build-out: it is a confirmed, qualified supplier to some of the world's largest data-center operators while declining, with studied corporate discretion, to name most of them. The company's IR disclosures and public filings as of the frozen snapshot date identify only two data-center relationships by name — Alibaba and, indirectly via Morgan Stanley research, Super Micro Computer. Every other hyperscaler relationship exists in the documentary record as inference, trade-press attribution, or the pointed non-denial of a company whose share price has re-rated nearly 500% on the expectation that such relationships are real and large.

The Alibaba relationship dates to 2018, when Kaori's coolant distribution units passed high-pressure validation testing during the Double Eleven Shopping Festival — a stress test that, given the commercial stakes of that event, carried the weight of a hyperscale qualification run. The exercise was formative: it demonstrated that Kaori's vacuum-brazed CDU cores could sustain the thermal and hydraulic demands of a live, high-density compute cluster, and it gave the company a reference it could take, obliquely, into subsequent sales conversations with other operators.

The Supermicro identification is the more commercially significant disclosure, precisely because it is one step removed from Kaori itself. [Morgan Stanley research published in 2024](https://stockanalysis.com/quote/tpe/8996/) named Kaori as a key CDU and manifold supplier for Supermicro's GB200 NVL72 liquid cooling platform — the primary delivery vehicle for NVIDIA's Blackwell AI accelerators. Because Supermicro itself serves Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services, and other hyperscale customers as an ODM partner, Kaori's components reach those operators' data-center floors without any of the customer names appearing in a Kaori filing. The supply chain is, by design, opaque.

What Kaori's commercial calendar reveals, however, is an active and escalating customer development campaign.
